words.definition: To praise someone or something highly, often in a public or formal way.
words.example: Critics lauded the young pianist for a performance of startling maturity.
words.mnemonic: LAUD sounds like 'loud' — you say loud, ringing praise about someone.

words.definition: To praise someone or something highly and enthusiastically.
words.example: At the retirement dinner, colleagues stood one by one to extol her decades of quiet, tireless service.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'ex-toll' — ring the bells (toll) to celebrate and praise someone loudly.

words.definition: To speak or write in high praise of a person, especially one who has died.
words.example: The pastor eulogized the fallen soldier before a silent, grieving congregation.
words.mnemonic: EU (good) + LOGY (words) — 'good words' spoken over someone, as at a funeral.

words.definition: A formal speech or piece of writing that expresses elaborate, lofty praise.
words.example: Her retirement dinner ended with a panegyric so glowing it left her blushing.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'pan' + 'lyric' — a whole pan piled high with lyrical flattery.

words.definition: A piece of warm, formal praise expressed in speech or writing.
words.example: The award came with a lengthy encomium listing every one of her achievements.
words.mnemonic: EN-COME-ee-um — friends 'come' to heap warm praise all over you.

words.definition: An award or public expression of approval given for achievement.
words.example: Winning the national prize was the highest accolade of her long career.
words.mnemonic: A knight received the accolade — a tap on the shoulder with a sword — as his top honor.

words.definition: An enthusiastic expression of approval, often in the form of applause.
words.example: The surprise ending earned the film plaudits from even its harshest reviewers.
words.mnemonic: PLAUDIT hides 'applaud' — both come from Latin plaudere, to clap.

words.definition: To promote or boast about something publicly to attract attention or buyers.
words.example: The salesman touted the blender as capable of replacing every gadget in the kitchen.
words.mnemonic: TOUT rhymes with 'shout' — you shout out how great your product is.

words.definition: To boast about or show off something in a proud, self-satisfied way.
words.example: He vaunted his connections to important people at every dinner party.
words.mnemonic: VAUNT rhymes with 'flaunt' — to vaunt is to flaunt something with your words.

words.definition: To treat a person as very important, famous, or celebrated.
words.example: After the discovery, the once-obscure scientist was lionized by the press.
words.mnemonic: LION-ize — treat someone like the lion, the celebrated king of the jungle.

words.definition: To raise someone to a higher rank, or to praise them very highly.
words.example: The revolution exalted a humble farmer to the rank of national hero.
words.mnemonic: EX + ALT (altitude) — to lift someone up to a great height.

words.definition: Excessive admiration or flattery directed at someone.
words.example: The pop star basked in the adulation of thousands of screaming fans.
words.mnemonic: ADORE + OVATION → adulation: an adoring ovation heaped on someone.

words.definition: To praise someone formally or officially for something they have done.
words.example: The officer was commended for bravery during the rescue.
words.mnemonic: COMMEND holds 'commendable' — worthy of official praise.

words.definition: Enthusiastic public approval and praise.
words.example: Her debut novel won critical acclaim and a shelf of awards.
words.mnemonic: AC + CLAIM — the crowd loudly 'claims' aloud how great you are.

words.definition: Special honor or respect shown publicly toward someone or something.
words.example: The director's film pays homage to the silent movies he loved as a child.
words.mnemonic: From 'homme' (man): a vassal pledged himself as his lord's man, a public sign of respect.

words.definition: Expressing strong approval or high praise for someone or something.
words.example: The critic's laudatory review kept the little theater sold out for a month.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'la-la' — the cheering sound of an approving crowd applauding.

words.definition: Formal or official acceptance and warm approval of something.
words.example: Her once-mocked theory finally won the approbation of the skeptical committee.
words.mnemonic: Begins like 'approve' — a-PROB-e it, then give it the nod.

words.definition: To describe something as grander or more admirable than it truly is.
words.example: Films that glorify war often skip over the suffering it leaves behind.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'glory' — to pack something full of glory it may not deserve.

words.definition: To make someone or something seem greater, richer, or more powerful, often falsely.
words.example: The ruler built colossal statues to aggrandize himself before the people.
words.mnemonic: Hides the word 'grand' — a-GRAND-ize means to puff up into something grand.

words.definition: To compliment someone excessively or insincerely, usually to win favor.
words.example: He tried to flatter the boss, praising every choice until she grew suspicious.
words.mnemonic: To 'butter up' — spread it on smooth and flat until the ego swells.

words.definition: To seek favor through exaggerated, servile affection or attention.
words.example: The waiters fawned over the celebrity, laughing at jokes that weren't funny.
words.mnemonic: Picture a baby deer (a fawn) nuzzling anyone nearby for attention.

words.definition: To persuade someone through steady coaxing, flattery, or gentle pressure.
words.example: She managed to cajole her brother into lending the car with promises of free gas.
words.mnemonic: Say it 'ca-JOLE' — coax someone into a jolly mood until they say yes.

words.definition: To behave in a humble, submissive way to gain forgiveness or favor.
words.example: After forgetting the anniversary, he had to grovel for a week before she forgave him.
words.mnemonic: Starts with 'grov-' like ground — crawling on the ground, begging.

words.definition: To criticize someone or something very harshly and openly.
words.example: The judge excoriated the company for dumping chemicals into the river.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'corium' (skin) — you verbally strip the skin right off someone.

words.definition: To scold or attack someone with strong, angry words.
words.example: The coach lambasted the team for their lazy play in the second half.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'lamb basted' — someone getting beaten and roasted with words.

words.definition: To spread damaging statements that make someone seem wicked or worthless.
words.example: The tabloids vilified the actor, printing rumors that wrecked his reputation.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'vil-' like 'villain' — to turn someone into the villain of the story.

words.definition: To attack someone with hateful, abusive language.
words.example: Once celebrated, the traitor was reviled by the very crowds who had cheered him.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'vile' — to keep calling someone vile, over and over.

words.definition: To speak of someone or something as if it has little value.
words.example: Don't disparage his efforts; he worked hard even if the result fell short.
words.mnemonic: Starts with 'dis' — to 'dis' someone, treating them as beneath equal (Latin par = equal).

words.definition: To express strong disapproval of something, or to play down its worth.
words.example: She tended to deprecate her own success, calling the award 'just luck'.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' (down) + 'prec' (pray/price) — to wish something down, lowering its price.

words.definition: To publicly condemn something as bad or wrong.
words.example: Activists gathered on the steps to decry the law they saw as unjust.
words.mnemonic: 'De-' + 'cry' — to cry out loudly against something in public.

words.definition: To officially and harshly express strong disapproval of someone's conduct.
words.example: The committee voted to censure the senator for accepting the bribe.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'censor' — both come down hard on what they judge wrong; to censure is to formally condemn.

words.definition: To express blame or disappointment toward someone for a fault.
words.example: She reproached him for forgetting her birthday yet again.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'roach' — picture pointing at a roach in someone's kitchen as you blame them for the mess.

words.definition: To criticize someone sharply and directly for a fault.
words.example: The coach rebuked the players for their lazy effort during practice.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 're-puke' — a sharp, forceful outburst of disapproval.

words.definition: To gently but firmly tell someone they have done something wrong.
words.example: The teacher reproved the student for whispering during the test.
words.mnemonic: Read it as 'remove approval' — to reprove is to signal you no longer approve.

words.definition: To scold someone severely and at length for a wrongdoing.
words.example: His mother upbraided him for staying out all night without calling.
words.mnemonic: 'Up-braid' — imagine someone yanking your hair up into a braid while loudly telling you off.

words.definition: To formally and sternly express disapproval of someone's actions.
words.example: The officer received a written reprimand for ignoring safety protocol.
words.mnemonic: Ends in 'command' — a superior's stern command about your mistake.

words.definition: To mildly scold or express annoyance at someone.
words.example: Grandma chided us for tracking mud across her clean floor.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'hide' — a scolded child wants to run off and hide.

words.definition: To warn or advise someone firmly about a fault or danger.
words.example: The judge admonished the witness to answer only the questions asked.
words.mnemonic: Latin root 'monere' = to warn (as in 'monitor'); think A-Dad's-warning.

words.definition: To angrily criticize someone loudly and at great length.
words.example: The chef berated the new cook until he nearly quit on his first day.
words.mnemonic: 'Be-RATE' — imagine someone shouting a terrible rating at you over and over.

words.definition: To criticize or punish someone harshly for wrongdoing.
words.example: The captain chastised his crew for abandoning their posts.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'chase-ties' — chasing someone down to tie them back into line.

words.definition: To attack someone with harsh, bitter, and abusive language.
words.example: The columnist vituperated against his rivals in every article he published.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'viper' inside it — spitting venomous, abusive words like a snake.

words.definition: To say harmful and untrue things about someone.
words.example: Rivals maligned her with rumors she could never fully disprove.
words.mnemonic: 'Mal' means bad (malice, malignant) — to speak evil of someone.

words.definition: To harm someone's reputation by making false statements about them.
words.example: He sued the tabloid for defaming him with a fabricated scandal.
words.mnemonic: 'De' (remove) + 'fame' — to strip away someone's good name.

words.definition: To make a false spoken statement that damages someone's reputation.
words.example: She was accused of slandering her neighbor by telling everyone he was a thief.
words.mnemonic: Slander = Spoken lie (both start with S); libel is written.

words.definition: A false written statement published to damage someone's reputation.
words.example: The magazine was found guilty of libel after printing lies about the actor.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'label' — a false written label stuck on someone; libeL and writtenL both end in L.

words.definition: To damage a person's reputation by making false and malicious statements about them.
words.example: Rivals sought to traduce her, spreading lies about bribes she had never taken.
words.mnemonic: From Latin traducere, 'to lead across' — as if parading someone across town in disgrace.

words.definition: To mock or express contempt for someone, treating them as laughably worthless.
words.example: The critics derided his first film, laughing openly at its wooden acting.
words.mnemonic: De- (down) + ride — to 'ride down' on someone, putting them beneath you.

words.definition: To make fun of someone cruelly so that they appear foolish.
words.example: Classmates ridiculed his stutter until he dreaded speaking aloud.
words.mnemonic: Shares its stem with 'ridiculous' — to ridicule is to make someone seem ridiculous.

words.definition: To publicly mock a person or institution with humorous, exaggerated writing or drawings.
words.example: The cartoonist lampooned the mayor, drawing him as a bloated toad on a throne.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'lamp' + 'harpoon' — you harpoon your target and hold them up under a lamp for all to laugh at.

words.definition: To use humor and irony to expose and criticize people's faults or society's flaws.
words.example: The novel satirizes greedy bankers, dressing them as pigs feasting at a golden trough.
words.mnemonic: Think of a 'sat-tire' that slowly deflates a pompous target with wit.

words.definition: To shout rude, mocking remarks at someone in a scornful way.
words.example: The crowd jeered at the referee, booing every call he made.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'sneer' — a jeer is a crowd's cheer twisted sour into a sneer.

words.definition: To speak about something with mocking contempt, treating it as ridiculous or worthless.
words.example: When she shared her plan to sail around the world alone, her coworkers began to scoff at the idea.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'scoff' as in scoffing down food dismissively — picture someone tossing off a rude 'pfft' while brushing crumbs aside.

words.definition: A taunting, sarcastic remark meant to belittle another person.
words.example: He couldn't resist a gibe about his brother's terrible parking.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'jibe' — a verbal jab, like a sailboat's boom swinging round to knock you sideways.

words.definition: To provoke or upset someone with insulting, mocking remarks.
words.example: The bullies taunted him about his hand-me-down shoes until he cried.
words.mnemonic: Taunt rhymes with 'haunt' — cruel taunts haunt you long after they're said.

words.definition: To publicly attack and humiliate someone, exposing them to widespread scorn.
words.example: The tabloids pilloried the actor for weeks after his careless comment.
words.mnemonic: A pillory was a wooden frame that locked a person's head and hands in the town square for public mockery.

words.definition: Severely and harshly critical in a way that wounds.
words.example: The reviewer wrote a scathing takedown that left the chef in tears.
words.mnemonic: Nearly 'scalding' — scathing words are hot enough to scald and leave a burn.

words.definition: Bitterly sarcastic and cutting in speech; also chemically able to burn.
words.example: Her caustic wit could reduce a confident speaker to silence.
words.mnemonic: Caustic soda burns skin — caustic remarks burn feelings the same way.

words.definition: Expressed forcefully and with sharp, effective insight.
words.example: Her trenchant analysis cut straight to the flaw everyone else had missed.
words.mnemonic: From French trancher, 'to slice' — a trenchant point carves a clean trench through confusion.

words.definition: Sharply sarcastic or bitingly critical, often in a darkly humorous way.
words.example: His mordant humor at funerals made mourners laugh despite themselves.
words.mnemonic: From Latin mordere, 'to bite' (as in 'morsel') — mordant wit sinks its teeth in.

words.definition: Filled with bitter, savage hostility or harsh criticism.
words.example: The debate turned vitriolic, each candidate spitting personal insults.
words.mnemonic: Vitriol is an old name for sulfuric acid — vitriolic words are acid poured on a person.

words.definition: Harsh, abusive language used to attack or criticize someone.
words.example: His speech dissolved into pure invective, hurling insults at every rival on stage.
words.mnemonic: IN-VECTIVE — like a VECTOR (guided missile) of insults aimed straight at you.

words.definition: A long, angry speech that bitterly criticizes something or someone.
words.example: The professor launched into a twenty-minute diatribe against standardized testing.
words.mnemonic: DIE-a-tribe: picture an angry TRIBE shouting until they nearly DIE ranting.

words.definition: A long outburst of angry, scolding, or critical words.
words.example: When the waiter spilled the wine, the customer erupted into a furious tirade.
words.mnemonic: TIRADE sounds like 'tired' — the listener gets TIRED of the endless angry speech.

words.definition: A strong written or spoken argument attacking or defending an opinion.
words.example: Her polemic against modern architecture provoked furious letters from every critic in town.
words.mnemonic: POLE-mic: grab a MIC on a POLE and fight fiercely for your side (Greek 'polemos' = war).

words.definition: A feeling that someone or something is unworthy of any respect.
words.example: She looked at the cheap imitation with obvious disdain and set it aside.
words.mnemonic: To 'DIS' someone — treat them as beneath you, nose turned up in DISdain.

words.definition: Open contempt or strong dislike shown toward someone considered beneath you.
words.example: He poured scorn on their plan, calling it naive and doomed.
words.mnemonic: SCORN sounds like 'scorch' — you scorch someone with burning contempt.

words.definition: Mockery or ridicule that makes someone or something seem foolish.
words.example: His suggestion was met with hoots of derision from the crowd.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'RIS' (Latin 'ridere', to laugh) — laughing AT someone to belittle them.

words.definition: A false or damaging remark that harms someone's reputation.
words.example: He sued the newspaper for casting aspersions on his honesty.
words.mnemonic: A-SPER-SION: imagine a SPURT of poison sprayed onto someone's good name.

words.definition: To complain or find fault continually about small, unimportant things.
words.example: Grandpa carps about the thermostat every single time he visits.
words.mnemonic: Picture a CARP fish endlessly opening its mouth — nag, nag, nag about nothing.

words.definition: To raise petty, unnecessary objections over minor details.
words.example: Rather than approve the design, the committee caviled over the font size.
words.mnemonic: CAVIL sounds like 'cavity' — a tiny hole you keep poking at with trivial complaints.

words.definition: To argue about small, unimportant details instead of the main point.
words.example: Let's not quibble over who pays the tip — the dinner was wonderful.
words.mnemonic: QUIBBLE rhymes with 'nibble' — you nibble at tiny details instead of the big issue.

words.definition: To express strong disapproval of something considered wrong or evil.
words.example: World leaders quickly condemned the attack as a crime against humanity.
words.mnemonic: CON-DEMN sounds like 'con-DAMN' — you DAMN the con(vict), declaring them guilty.

words.definition: To publicly declare someone or something to be wrong or evil.
words.example: The senator stood before cameras to denounce the corruption in her own party.
words.mnemonic: DE-NOUNCE ~ 'announce' — you publicly ANNOUNCE that someone is bad (DE = down on them).

words.definition: To formally charge someone with committing a crime.
words.example: A grand jury voted to indict the executive on fraud charges.
words.mnemonic: Pronounced 'in-DITE': think IN + DICTate — the court DICTates the crimes against you.

words.definition: A speech or writing that highly praises someone, often after death.
words.example: At the funeral, her son delivered a moving eulogy about her lifelong kindness.
words.mnemonic: EU ('good', Greek) + LOGY ('words') = GOOD WORDS spoken about a person.

words.definition: To hold someone or something in deep respect and admiration.
words.example: Students still revere the old professor who shaped this department decades ago.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'reverend' — you look up to a reverend with deep respect.

words.definition: Respect and high regard felt for someone because of their qualities.
words.example: Her colleagues held her in such high esteem that they named the prize after her.
words.mnemonic: e-STEAM: a good reputation rises like steam and lifts you up.

words.definition: An act, gift, or statement showing gratitude, respect, or admiration.
words.example: The concert was a tribute to the drummer who had passed away that spring.
words.mnemonic: A 'tribe' gathers to pay tribute to its chief.

words.definition: Praise and recognition given for an achievement.
words.example: The team earned kudos from the mayor for cleaning up the neglected river.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'you dos' — well-done deeds earn you the applause.

words.definition: Dull, ordinary, and lacking imagination or excitement.
words.example: She dreamed of far-off adventures, but her prosaic office routine offered none.
words.mnemonic: Think 'prose' versus poetry — plain prose, never lyrical verse.

words.definition: Severe or plain in appearance, without comfort or decoration.
words.example: The monks lived in austere cells holding only a bed and a candle.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'oh, stern' — this look is stern and bare.

words.definition: Having mixed or conflicting feelings about something at the same time.
words.example: He felt ambivalent about the promotion, glad for the raise but dreading the travel.
words.mnemonic: 'Ambi-' means both (as in ambidextrous) — you feel both ways at once.

words.definition: Mysterious and understood by only a few people with special knowledge.
words.example: The wizard guarded his arcane spells from the ordinary villagers below.
words.mnemonic: 'Ark' + 'cane' — secret knowledge locked in an ancient ark.

words.definition: Done quickly with little attention to detail.
words.example: A cursory glance at the contract made her miss the hidden fee entirely.
words.mnemonic: Like a 'cursor' racing across the screen — a fast, shallow pass.

words.definition: Insisting one's opinions are certainly true and refusing any debate.
words.example: The dogmatic coach would not hear any strategy but his own.
words.mnemonic: A 'dog' clamped on a bone — it won't let go of its views.

words.definition: Made up of elements chosen from many different sources or styles.
words.example: Her eclectic playlist jumped from opera to hip-hop to old jazz.
words.mnemonic: 'Elect' the best bits from everywhere and mix them together.

words.definition: Lacking flavor, interest, or liveliness; bland and boring.
words.example: The soup was so insipid that she reached for the salt at once.
words.mnemonic: 'In-sip-id' — take a sip and there is no taste at all.

words.definition: Not expressed directly; slanting rather than straight to the point.
words.example: Instead of answering, he gave an oblique hint and changed the subject.
words.mnemonic: An oblique line leans at a slant — never straight ahead.

words.definition: Not able to be seen through, or very difficult to understand.
words.example: The bathroom window was opaque, letting in light while hiding the room.
words.mnemonic: 'O-pake' — a cake so thick that no light gets through it.

words.definition: Dealing with problems in a practical, realistic way rather than idealistically.
words.example: Rather than chase a perfect plan, she took a pragmatic approach and fixed what she could.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'practical' — a pragmatic person keeps it practical.
